Emma Cumiford Datasheet as part of Project SBWB for Team 208

Submission: October 28, 2026

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: This datasheet documents the design process for the actuation and motor control portion of Project SBWB's Self-Balancing Work Bench.

docs.title: Project Summary
docs.text: Project SBWB is a self-balancing work bench that keeps its work surface level automatically. Sensing subsystems measure the bench's position, and the actuation subsystem physically adjusts the bench in response. My subsystem provides that motion: it receives signals from my teammates' boards, such as the distance-sensing subsystem, and drives a 6 V linear actuator to move the bench into balance. For a full overview of the project, including every team member's subsystem, see our team report.

docs.title: My Contribution
docs.text:
My role on the team covers two main areas:

  • Actuation board: designing the hardware that physically adjusts the bench, built around a 5-12 V linear actuator
  • Motor control: using an H-bridge motor driver to let a PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano control the actuator's direction and speed through PWM.

To help navigate this datasheet:

  • For an overview of how the subsystem's components connect, see the Block Diagram section.
  • For the reasoning behind part choices such as the actuator, see the Component Selection section.
  • For the materials used to build the subsystem, see the "BOM" section.
  • For the electrical design, see the Schematic section.
  • For how power will be distributed, see the Power Budget section.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
This block diagram shows how my individual subsystem, the actuator control board, fits into the team project. It shows how power, control signals, and team connections flow between the microcontroller, the motor driver, and the actuator.

  • Microcontroller: A PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano controls the subsystem. It generates a PWM signal on pin RA2 to drive the motor, and uses digital I/O pins (RA1, RB2, RD0, RD1) to communicate with the rest of the team.
  • Actuator: A VEVOR OK648 12 V linear actuator provides the system's mechanical motion.
  • Motor driver: A FAN8011N H-bridge receives the 3.3 V PWM signal from the microcontroller on IN1. It switches 12 V DC to the actuator, letting the low-power microcontroller control the high-power motor.
  • Power levels:
  • 6 V DC: powers the actuator through the H-bridge
  • 3.3 V: used for all logic-level signals between the microcontroller, the H-bridge, and the team connectors
  • Power source: An external 12 V DC supply powers the board. It feeds the actuator directly through the H-bridge and is regulated down for the logic circuitry.
  • Sensor: This subsystem has no sensor of its own. It acts on commands and data that come from teammates' boards through the team connectors.
  • Team connections: Two 8-pin connectors link this board to the rest of the team's system. On each one, pins 1–2 carry 3.3 V digital signals to the microcontroller (RA1/RB2 on the first, RD0/RD1 on the second), and pin 8 provides a shared ground.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The motor control board only needs two main components: a motor driver (H-bridge) and an actuator. The microcontroller sends forward/reverse logic signals to the H-bridge. The H-bridge switches power from the supply to the actuator and controls which direction it moves. Apart from these two parts, the board only needs basic support components such as decoupling capacitors, a power input, and connectors.

Because the two parts have to work together electrically, choosing one limits the options for the other. We chose the FAN8100N dual H-bridge first because our professor recommended it, it accepts 3.3 V and 5 V logic directly from the microcontroller, and its through-hole DIP package is easy to put on a PCB. However, the FAN8100N is a low-voltage driver. Its motor supply is rated for 1.8–9 V, and each channel can supply up to 1.5 A peak.

These limits ruled out most of the actuators we looked at. Typical linear actuators, including the two VEVOR models we compared, run on 12 V, and Option 1 draws up to 5 A. Both are above the FAN8100N's ratings. The mini push-pull solenoid was the only option that fit. It runs on 5–12 V, draws only 0.58 A at 9 V (the manufacturer's recommended "best balance" setting), and connects with two wires. Its tradeoffs are a short 5 mm stroke, a low 40 g pull force, and on-times kept to about 1 second. Even so, it is the only actuator we found that works within the driver's voltage and current limits.

docs.title: Actuation
docs.text:
Option Pros Cons Option 1.VEVOR 12V Linear Actuator, 18 in stroke (OK648-1500N)$42.90/eachlink to product * High load capacity (330 lbs / 1500 N)* Current draw is documented (5 A)* Mounting brackets included* IP54 dust and splash protection * Requires 12 V, above the FAN8100N's 9 V limit* Draws up to 5 A, above the FAN8100N's 1.5 A rating* No built-in position feedback* Only a 25% duty cycle* Slow (0.19 in/s) and physically large Option 2.VEVOR 12V High-Speed Linear Actuator, 20 in stroke (OK648-1000N)$43.90/eachlink to product * Fast travel speed (0.55 in/s)* Quiet (≤50 dB)* Built-in limit switches stop the motor at the ends of travel* IP54 dust and splash protection * Requires 12 V, above the FAN8100N's 9 V limit* Current draw not listed, so H-bridge sizing is uncertain* Lower load capacity than Option 1 (220 lbs / 1000 N)* No built-in position feedback* Long (24.6 in retracted body) Option 3.Mini DC Push-Pull Solenoid, 5 mm (0.2 in) stroke (DS-0420S) \([\)15.96/each]/eachlink to product * Runs on 5–12 V DC, so it works on the board's 9 V supply* Low current draw (0.40 A at 6 V, 0.58 A at 9 V, 0.77 A at 12 V)* Small and light (12 x 11 x 38.2 mm, 13.5 g)* Simple 2-wire connection (90 mm cable) * Very short stroke (5 mm)* Low pull force (40 g max)* Short-term use only: max ~1 s continuous on-time to avoid overheating* Runs hotter at higher voltages

Choice: Option 3: Mini DC Push-Pull Solenoid, 5 mm (0.2 in) stroke

Rationale: Option 1 was our first choice because of its high load capacity (330 lbs / 1500 N) and fully documented specifications, but it needs 12 V and up to 5 A, which is more than our motor driver can supply. Option 2 has the same 12 V problem and does not list its current draw. The solenoid was the only option that works within the H-bridge's limits. It runs on the board's 9 V supply, so the H-bridge can drive it directly without a separate power stage or converter. At 9 V it draws 0.58 A, which is within the FAN8100N's 1.5 A per-channel rating. Its 40 g pull force and 5 mm stroke are enough for a demonstration model. It would not be strong enough for a full-scale work bench, but it is the only choice compatible with our motor control board, which makes it the right fit for this design.

docs.title: Control
docs.text:
Option Pros Cons Option 1.Fairchild/onsemi FAN8100N Low-Voltage 2-Channel DC Motor Driver (12-DIP)$[price]/eachlink to product * Two full H-bridge channels in one chip, so it can drive a brushed DC motor forward, reverse, and brake* Works directly with 3.3 V and 5 V microcontroller logic* Simple parallel control interface (forward/reverse inputs per channel)* Through-hole DIP package, which is easy to solder and prototype on a PCB* Recommended by our professor * Motor supply rated 1.8–9 V (10.5 V absolute max), which rules out 12 V actuators* Peak output current is only 1.5 A per channel* Marked obsolete; sold through Rochester Electronics on DigiKey Marketplace* Bipolar transistors, so it has more voltage drop and heat than a MOSFET driver

Choice: Option 1: Fairchild/onsemi FAN8100N 2-Channel DC Motor Driver

Rationale: The FAN8100N puts two full H-bridge channels in a single through-hole IC, so the board can drive the actuator forward, in reverse, and brake it without discrete transistors. Its inputs accept 3.3 V and 5 V logic, so it connects directly to the microcontroller's GPIO pins. The DIP package is easy to place and solder on our PCB. Our professor also recommended this driver to another student for a similar design, which gives us confidence it is suitable for a class motor control board. Its main limits are a 9 V maximum operating supply and a 1.5 A peak output per channel, so the actuator's voltage and current draw must stay within those ratings.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
This Bill of Materials documents Project SBWB’s (Self-Balancing Work Bench) actuation and motor control board. It lists every part needed for one prototype unit, along with its manufacturer, supplier and datasheet. The board takes 12 VDC from a wall adapter through a barrel jack, regulates it down to 5 V for the logic, and uses an on-board H-bridge motor driver IC to drive the linear actuator under control of the microcontroller. Status LEDs and a pushbutton are included for indication and manual input. This serves as documentation of the parts that make up the subsystem, so it can be referred to and replicated.

Some important notes: Unit Quantity is how many of each component are in one module. Unit Prototype Cost is the cost of one of that component, and Total Prototype Cost is what it costs to buy enough of that part for one complete prototype. Parts listed as $0.00 come from the PRLTA 109 lab stock. # Ordered counts extra parts bought for breadboarding and replacements, not the number the board needs. The Date Ordered, # Received and Surplus columns track orders as they come in.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
This schematic shows the actuation and motor control board for Project SBWB (Self-Balancing Work Bench). The board's job is to move the actuator when the microcontroller tells it to. Power comes in at 12 V DC through a barrel jack, passes through a fuse, and is regulated down to 5 V by an LM7805 to power the logic. The Curiosity Nano microcontroller sends forward and reverse signals to a FAN8100N H-bridge motor driver, which switches power to the actuator through the motor connector. Three headers carry the microcontroller's I/O pins off the board so other subsystems, such as the distance-sensing board, can connect. A power indicator LED, two test points, a test pin header, a debug LED, and a debug push button make the board easier to test and troubleshoot. This schematic documents how the subsystem is wired, so it can be referred to, built, and replicated.

Figure ##: Showing Emma's Schematic

docs.title: Schematic Description
docs.text:
This schematic shows the actuation and motor control board for Project SBWB. The board takes 12 V DC in, regulates it to 5 V for the logic, and uses a FAN8100N H-bridge driver to drive the actuator under control of the microcontroller. It is split into the following blocks.

Microcontroller: The Curiosity Nano (EGR304 board) is the main controller. Its 5 V and ground pins connect to the board's supply rails, and C4 (0.1 µF) decouples its supply. Its I/O pins are labeled with net names (RA, RB, RC, RD) that go to the connectors, the motor driver, and the debug circuits.

Connectors (J4, J5, J6): Three 702460801 headers bring the microcontroller's I/O pins off the board so other subsystems, such as the team's distance-sensing board, can connect. Each header carries digital I/O lines and a ground. J6 is an extra header for added signals.

Power Supply: 12 V comes in through the barrel jack (J1). F1 (2.5 A) protects the board from overcurrent. An LM7805 linear regulator steps 12 V down to 5 V for the logic. C1 (0.33 µF) on its input and C2 (0.1 µF) on its output keep it stable. D1, with current-limiting resistor R1 (330 Ω), is a power indicator LED that lights when 5 V is present. Test points TP1 (12 V input) and TP2 (5 V output) allow quick voltage checks with a multimeter.

Motor Driver: The FAN8100N H-bridge drives the actuator. Its logic supply (VCC) runs from 5 V, and its motor supplies (PVCCA, PVCCB) come from the motor supply rail. C3 decouples the supply. The microcontroller controls direction through FORWARDA (RA2) and REVERSEA (RA0): one input drives the actuator forward, the other reverses it, and both together brake it. Channel A's outputs (OUT1A, OUT2A) go to the motor connector J3. Channel B is unused.

Motor Connector (J3): A 2-pin connector carries OUT1A and OUT2A to the actuator.

Debugging LED: D2, with current-limiting resistor R2 (330 Ω), is driven by the LED DEBUG pin on the microcontroller. It lets the code show status visually during testing.

Debugging Push Button: SW1 connects the BUTTON DEBUG pin to ground when pressed. R3 (10 kΩ) pulls the pin up to 5 V, so the pin reads high normally and low when the button is pressed. This gives a manual input for testing the code.

Test Pins Connector (J7): A fourth 702460801 header collects the board's key test signals in one place. Pins 1 and 2 carry TP1 (12 V input after the fuse) and TP2 (5 V regulator output), and pins 3 and 4 carry MotorOut1 and MotorOut2 from the H-bridge. This lets the supply voltages and the motor driver outputs be checked with a multimeter or oscilloscope, or brought out to another board, without probing the components directly. The remaining pins are not connected.

Design Note: Unless stated otherwise, every resistor is rated for 1/4 W, every capacitor is rated for 50 V, and the fuse is rated for 2.5 A.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
A power budget lists every major component on the board, how much current each one can draw, and which power rail supplies it. The goal is to confirm that the voltage regulator and the external power supply can deliver enough current for everything on the board, with room to spare. Without this check, the board could brown out, reset, or overheat when the actuator turns on.

For the Project SBWB motor control board, I listed the three major components: the FAN8100N H-bridge motor driver, the DS-0420S solenoid actuator, and the Curiosity Nano microcontroller. I recorded each one's supply voltage range and maximum current draw, then added them up on the 5 V rail and applied a 25% safety margin. I then picked a 5 V regulator (L7805ABV-DG) and a plug-in wall supply (SWI18-9-N-P5) that can handle that load.

Figure 1: Power budget for the Project SBWB motor control board

docs.title: Conclusions
docs.text:
The power budget shows that the selected parts can power the board. The components on the 5 V rail draw a subtotal of 1117.5 mA. With a 25% safety margin, the 5 V rail requires 1396.875 mA. The L7805ABV-DG regulator can supply up to 1500 mA, which leaves 103.125 mA of extra current on the 5 V rail.

The 9 V, 2200 mA plug-in wall supply powers the regulator. Even if the regulator draws its full 1500 mA, the wall supply still has 700 mA available. The original 650 mA wall supply was not enough to power the board, which is why it was replaced with the 2.2 A supply. The budget is conservative because it uses each part's absolute maximum current, so the real current draw during normal operation will be lower.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
This page documents the printed circuit board (PCB) layout for the actuation and motor control board of Project SBWB (Self-Balancing Work Bench). The layout was created in KiCad 10 from the updated schematic on the Schematics page and manufactured by PCBWay as a two-layer board. The final design passes the KiCad Design Rules Check (DRC) with zero errors and was checked with the JLCDFM manufacturability tool before ordering.

The board takes 12 V DC in through a switched barrel jack and a 2.5 A fuse. An LM7805 regulates it to 5 V for the logic, and a Curiosity Nano microcontroller drives the actuator through a FAN8100N H-bridge. Headers along the right edge connect the board to the rest of the team's system.

docs.title: Board Specifications
docs.text: Specification Requirement This Design Copper layers 2 (top and bottom) 2 Board size ≤ 100 mm × 100 mm 42.5 mm × 100 mm Copper weight 0.5 oz/ft² (design basis) Designed for 0.5 oz/ft², manufactured at 1 oz/ft² Power and ground trace width ≥ 40 mil, sized with a calculator 2.13 mm (83.9 mil) Signal trace width Fabricator minimum 0.2 mm (about 8 mil) Power and ground planes Both sides +5V pour (top), ground pour (bottom) Via annular ring Fabricator minimum 0.2 mm Initials on top copper Large, bold font "EC" Layer labels "top", "bottom", group name "Top", "Bottom", "Group 208 SBWB Motor Control Board" Fabrication Two-layer FR-4 FR-4, 1.6 mm, green soldermask, top silkscreen (PCBWay) DRC 0 errors 0 errors, 0 warnings, 0 unconnected pads

docs.title: Layout Design Decisions
docs.text:
Component Placement: The board is a narrow 42.5 mm × 100 mm layout. The Curiosity Nano runs along the left edge, so its pins can fan out to the right toward the rest of the circuit. The FAN8100N H-bridge sits at the top center, close to the microcontroller pins that drive it (FORWARDA on RA2 and REVERSEA on RA0). The four 702460801 headers (J7, J6, J5, J4) line the right edge from top to bottom. The debug LED (D2) and fuse (F1) sit in the middle of the board, and resistors R1–R3 are in the lower center. The power section is along the bottom: the barrel jack (J1) and power LED (D1) on the lower left, and the LM7805 regulator with capacitors C1–C4 on the lower right. The debug push button (SW1) is at the bottom center.

Power Routing: Trace widths were sized with the Advanced Circuits trace width calculator, using the 2.5 A fuse rating, 0.5 oz/ft² copper, external layers, and a 10 °C temperature rise. The calculator gave a required width of 83.7 mil (about 2.13 mm). All power and ground traces (12 V input, fuse, motor outputs, 5 V, and ground) are 2.13 mm (83.9 mil) wide. This meets the calculated requirement and is more than twice the 40 mil checklist minimum. Because the board was manufactured with 1 oz copper instead of the 0.5 oz used in the calculation, the traces have extra current margin. Signal traces are 0.2 mm (about 8 mil).

Power and Ground Planes: The top copper layer has a +5V power pour and the bottom copper layer has a ground (Earth) pour. The pours give the logic supply and its return path a low-impedance path across the whole board.

Decoupling Capacitors: C1 (0.33 µF) and C2 (0.1 µF) are the input and output capacitors for the LM7805. C3 (0.1 µF) is the bypass capacitor for the FAN8100N H-bridge, and C4 (0.1 µF) is the bypass capacitor for the Curiosity Nano. All four capacitors are grouped in the lower right next to the LM7805.

Connectors: J4, J5, and J6 are 702460801 headers that connect this board to the other subsystems. J7 is a 702460801 header that serves as both the test header and the actuator connection: pins 3 and 4 carry MotorOut1 and MotorOut2 from the H-bridge. All connectors are along the board edges, so cables can plug in without crossing over other parts, and all are through-hole for mechanical strength.

Testing and Debugging: J7 brings TP1 (12 V after the fuse), TP2 (5 V), and both motor outputs to one header, so the board can be probed without touching components. The debug LED (D2, with R2) and the debug push button (SW1, with a 10 kΩ pull-up R3) can be used to test the microcontroller code. The power LED (D1, with R1) shows when the board has power.

Routing Practices: The board was routed with a combination of the autorouter and hand routing. The power and ground traces were routed by hand. Vias were enlarged to give a 0.2 mm annular ring for reliable manufacturing.

docs.title: Design Rules Check (DRC)
docs.text:
The final design passes the KiCad DRC with 0 errors, 0 warnings, and 0 unconnected pads. Two cosmetic silkscreen warnings were reviewed and excluded.

Figure 5: KiCad DRC results showing zero errors

docs.title: Manufacturing Verification
docs.text:
The Gerber and drill files were checked with the JLCDFM online DFM tool before ordering from PCBWay. All routing, trace width and spacing, annular ring, hole clearance, slot, and drill checks passed (all 100 holes rated Good). The remaining flags are false positives:

  • "THT to SMD": JLCDFM does not have the schematic, so it reads a round through-hole pad next to the barrel jack's slotted pads (0.91 mm apart) as a via. This check only matters for automated assembly, and this board is hand-soldered.
  • Silkscreen to pad: Some footprint outline lines touch pads. The fabricator clips these automatically.

Custom footprints are stored in the FootprintLib_EGR304_EC footprint library, which is included in the KiCad project zip.
